subject: combined-science

items.q: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of an unknown gas. Which observation shows that the gas is hydrogen?
items.correct: The gas burns rapidly with a pop sound
items.why: Both tests use a wooden splint, so the two procedures and their results are swapped in memory. Learn the pairs together: burning splint plus pop is hydrogen; glowing splint plus relight is oxygen.
items.random_wrong: The splint is put out straight away

items.q: Which procedure and result together make up the test for hydrogen?
items.correct: A burning splint at the open end gives a pop
items.misconception: A glowing splint is inserted and then relights
items.why: Both tests use a wooden splint, so the two procedures and their results are swapped in memory. Learn the pairs together: burning splint plus pop is hydrogen; glowing splint plus relight is oxygen.
items.random_wrong: Damp litmus paper is held in it and whitens

items.q: A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of gas and the splint relights. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: The gas is oxygen, as it relights the splint
items.misconception: The gas is carbon dioxide, as it relights splints
items.why: Carbon dioxide and oxygen are the two gases tested most often, so the observation is attached to the wrong one. Only oxygen relights the glowing splint; carbon dioxide is identified by limewater turning milky.
items.random_wrong: The relighting shows the gas is burning itself

items.q: Which splint and which result are used to identify oxygen?
items.misconception: A burning splint that then relights
items.why: A burning splint is the more familiar piece of practical work, and a splint burning more brightly in oxygen looks like a sensible result. The specification states that the oxygen test uses a glowing splint inserted into the tube, and that the splint relights.
items.random_wrong: A glowing splint that lights the gas

items.q: Limewater is used in the test for carbon dioxide. What is limewater?
items.correct: An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide
items.misconception: An aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide
items.why: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali met most often in class, so any alkaline solution is assumed to be that one. Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution: the calcium is what forms the milky solid when carbon dioxide is added.

items.q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. What is observed?
items.why: Milky and white sound like the same observation, so the carbon dioxide result is described in the language of the chlorine test. Limewater turns milky or cloudy because a white solid forms in it; nothing is bleached.
items.random_wrong: The limewater turns a bright yellow

items.q: Damp litmus paper is put into a test tube of chlorine gas. What happens to the paper?
items.correct: It is bleached and turns white
items.misconception: It turns bright red and stays red
items.why: Chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper to give an acidic solution, so a red colour can be seen first and students stop the observation there. The specification result is that damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
items.random_wrong: It turns green like the gas

items.q: Which observation identifies a gas as chlorine?
items.misconception: Dry litmus paper turns bright white
items.why: The word damp is treated as an unimportant practical detail rather than part of the stated test. The specification states that damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas and is bleached.
items.random_wrong: Damp litmus paper turns deep red

items.q: What happens to a burning splint held at the open end of a tube of hydrogen?
items.correct: The hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.
items.misconception: Students think the splint is simply put out, because the tube contains no oxygen.
items.why: They over-apply the rule that a flame needs oxygen and forget that the hydrogen itself burns in the air at the mouth of the tube. Hydrogen is the flammable gas here; it burns rapidly at the open end and the pop is heard.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the oxygen itself burn when the splint relights?
items.correct: No. The splint burns; the oxygen supports that burning.
items.misconception: Students think oxygen is a flammable gas that catches fire.
items.why: The words fire, burning and oxygen are used together so often that oxygen gets labelled as the fuel. Oxygen supports combustion; the fuel in this test is the wooden splint.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is limewater a solution of calcium carbonate?
items.correct: No. It is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.
items.misconception: Students think limewater is calcium carbonate solution.
items.why: They remember calcium carbonate from this test and confuse the insoluble product with the starting reagent. Calcium hydroxide is the dissolved reagent; the calcium carbonate formed is insoluble, which is why the solution goes cloudy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it?
items.misconception: Students think there is no visible change because carbon dioxide is a colourless gas.
items.why: They expect a colourless gas to give a colourless result, and think a positive test must mean a new colour. The change is not a colour change but a cloudiness: a white insoluble solid forms and makes the limewater milky.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does chlorine turn litmus paper blue?
items.correct: No. The litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
items.misconception: Students think chlorine is alkaline and so turns litmus blue.
items.why: Household bleach is an alkaline product associated with chlorine, so the alkali label is transferred to the gas. The chlorine test result is a loss of colour to white, not a blue colour.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
